chunks: Power sequencing: why, order, timing. The question: What is power sequencing? When/why is it needed? How is the sequence determined?
How much time between each rail turning on/off is needed?
Power sequencing means turning a system's supply voltages (its "rails") on and off in a controlled order and with controlled timing.
Many chips have several rails, such as a low-voltage core and a higher-voltage I/O ring.
Powering them in the wrong order can push current through paths that were never meant to carry it. Sequencing keeps the chip safe and starting in a known state.
It is like getting dressed: socks go on before shoes. You could force it the other way, but it works badly and you might damage something.
The difference is that you can see the right order for clothes. For chips, the datasheet tells you the order, and common sense can mislead you.
Each rail starts only after the previous rail's power-good is asserted (plus about 2 milliseconds of settling), and reset is held low until every rail has been valid for about 10 milliseconds.
Each ramp is monotonic and takes a few ms, which keeps inrush ( I equals C dV over dt ) under control. All times here are illustrative.
Rail: one supply voltage in the system, such as 1. 0 volts or 3. 3 volts. Power domain: a part of a chip fed by its own rail, such as the core or the I/O.
ESD diode: a protection diode on each pin that guards against static shocks. It can also conduct if the wrong rail is up first.
Power-good (PG): a signal that says a rail has reached a valid level.
Reset: a signal that holds a chip in a known state until all rails are stable ("Design a power architecture from a spec").
A chip has a 1. 0 volts core and a 3. 3 volts I/O rail. Its datasheet says the I/O voltage must not exceed the core voltage by more than 0. 3 volts. If 3.
3 volts comes up first, the I/O sits 3. 3 volts above a core that is still at 0 volts. That breaks the rule, and current can flow through the ESD diodes into the core.
So the core comes up first. Once its power-good signal says it is valid, the I/O rail starts. That is the whole idea.
"Power sequencing is controlling the order and timing of supply rails turning on and off.
It's needed because multi-rail chips can be damaged or left in undefined states if, say, the I/O is powered while the core isn't, since ESD diodes back-power the core or latch-up occurs.
The order comes from the datasheets: sequence sections and absolute max ratings like I/O not exceeding core by 0. 3 volts.
The timing is usually threshold-based using power-good, or a ramp-time window from the datasheet, with reset held until everything is stable, and power-down in reverse."
